Finally, models in the bottom-right quadrant (Frequent low performers) consistently achieve a low proportion of top-ranked forecasts and frequently rank among the weakest performers. For both diseases and metrics, models cluster along the anti-diagonal, with few models in the top-right corner, indicating that high inconsistency is uncommon. Focusing on FluSight (4A, 4B), TimesFM is in the top-left quadrant (Top performers), ranking in the bottom 30% in approximately 20% of forecasts while appearing in the top 30% in approximately 40% of forecasts for log WIS, and a lower number of forecasts in the top 30% for log AE (nearly 30%). Chronos-2 follows a similar pattern, though with a marginally higher bottom-rank frequency for log AE and a slightly lower top-rank proportion (around 30% for log WIS), positioning it on the boundary between the Top performers and the Consistent performers. For log WIS, Moirai-2 and TabPFN-TS patterns are similar to TimesFM and Chronos-2, falling in the top-left quadrant with high top-rank and low bottom-rank frequencies. For log AE, both models move toward the central region of the plot, indicating more moderate and mixed performance. TimeGPT is placed in the Frequent low performer quadrant for log WIS and in the top-left quadrant as a Top performer for log AE. The baseline model and Lag-Llama are consistently positioned in the Frequent low performer quadrant, with Lag-Llama approaching the bottom-right corner, reflecting a very high proportion of bottom-ranked forecasts. The ensemble is placed in the moderate quadrant for both log WIS and AE, yet stands out for its stability: it never ranks in the bottom 30%, despite not frequently reaching the top 30% as other models. Other individual models are scattered across all quadrants, with a subset reaching the top-left quadrant, indicating that some hub participants achieve consistently strong performance, comparable to or higher than that of the best-performing TSFMs. The CovidHub analysis (4C, 4D) shows consistent patterns. Chronos-2 and TabPFN-TS emerge as the most reliable TSFMs, both occupying top-to-moderate quadrants, while the baseline model and Lag-Llama remain the weakest performers. TimeGPT again confirms its metric-dependent performance: it achieves high top-rank frequency and the second-lowest bottom-rank frequency among TSFMs for log AE, yet shows a low-performer profile for log WIS. For CovidHub, TabPFN-TS records the lowest bottom-rank frequency for log WIS across the six TSFMs and a bottom-rank frequency for log AE comparable to TimeGPT, indicating consistent performance on both metrics. In this case, the ensemble achieves a top-rank proportion of more than 50% for log WIS and approximately 33% for log AE, while again rarely appearing in the bottom rankings, further confirming its consistent and reliable performance. Focusing on FluSight (Figs. 5C, 5D), most models perform better during the increase and stable phases, as indicated by the leftward shift of the orange and grey dots relative to the blue ones. This pattern holds across both TSFMs and hub participants, with Lag-Llama showing only a median ratio close to 1 in the stable phase for log WIS, and consistently above 1 across all other phases. TimeGPT shows notable phase-dependent inconsistency, especially for log WIS, performing strongly during the increase and large increase trends but falling below the baseline during decrease and large decrease trends. The ensemble remains the best-performing model across most epidemic phases: in terms of log WIS ratio, it reaches the first position for large increase and large decrease phases, the second position for the stable and decrease trends, where Moirai-2 outperforms it, and again the second position for the increase trend, following TimesFM; in terms of log AE ratio, it reaches the first position for the stable, decrease, and large decrease trends, the second position for large increase, following TabPFN-TS, and the third position for increase, following TimeGPT and TimesFM.

2.5 Evaluating performance across epidemic phases

Considering the CovidHub (Figs. 5E, 5F), similar phase-dependent patterns emerge, though the differences are less pronounced, as reflected by the closer clustering of the dots. This may partly reflect the smaller number of weeks classified as non-stable for COVID-19 relative to influenza (see Fig. 5B, top panel). For this reason, phase-specific medians do not diverge as clearly as in the FluSight analysis. The ensemble's outperformance is also more evident in this case, with its data point consistently positioned to the left of all other models across all epidemic phases, except for the large-increase trend. These results suggest that, when performance is disaggregated by epidemic phase, TSFMs do not outperform the ensemble and behave similarly to the other individual models contributing to the hub.

2.6 Retrospective evaluation of the 2024/25 season

To assess the robustness of our findings beyond a single epidemic season, we conducted a retrospective evaluation of the six TSFMs during the 2024/25 season under operational real-time forecasting conditions, which required using versioned data available at the time each forecast was made. Weekly forecasts were produced over 25 forecasting rounds, from November 30, 2024, through May 24, 2025, for both hubs. During this season, 48 models contributed to FluSight and 19 to CovidHub, with 38 and 10 models, respectively, eligible for evaluation. Full details and results are reported in the Supplementary Information (in Sec. S1 and Sec. S3). The overall performance patterns are broadly consistent with those observed for 2025/26. Chronos-2, TabPFN-TS, and TimesFM remain the most competitive TSFMs, never ranking in the bottom tertile for WIS or AE, and consistently outperforming the baseline across most U.S. jurisdictions for influenza and, in terms of WIS, for COVID-19. Chronos-2 performs best for influenza and TabPFN-TS for COVID-19. Lag-Llama ranks last among all evaluated models for both WIS and AE in both hubs. TimeGPT confirms its cross-metric inconsistency, with stronger point-forecast el) op m ios ge of are ng e 2, s d accuracy (AE) than probabilistic performance (WIS), particularly for influenza. Moirai-2 shows moderate performance across different settings. One notable difference from 2025/26 is the phase-dependent pattern: in 2024/25, models tended to perform better in decrease-trend phases than in increase-trend phases, especially for influenza, reversing the pattern observed in 2025/26 and suggesting season-specific differences in the forecast ability of each epidemic phase. Across both seasons and all analyses, the ensemble remains the strongest and most reliable forecasting strategy.

3 Discussion

In this work, we systematically evaluated six state-of-the-art TSFMs in an operational setting for short-term epidemic forecasting. The evaluation covered two respiratory disease targets, influenza and COVID-19 hospitalizations, and 53 locations (the U.S. national level and 52 U.S. jurisdictions). TSFMs were benchmarked against multi-model ensembles and individual models, including mechanistic, statistical, machine learning, and deep learning approaches. In addition, we assessed the robustness of our findings through a retrospective performance assessment of the 2024/25 season (Supplementary Information, Sec. S3).

TSFMs represent a potential opportunity for operational epidemic forecasting, offering ready access to state-of-the-art approaches without requiring the specialized expertise needed to build and maintain mechanistic or custom deep learning models. However, how their accuracy compared with that of the disease-specific models explicitly developed for this task remained unclear. Our analyses showed that the performance of the considered TSFMs is highly heterogeneous. Results suggest distinct performance profiles: Chronos-2, TimesFM, and TabPFN-TS emerge as the most competitive and reliable TSFMs across settings; TimeGPT shows metric-dependent performance, achieving strong point forecast accuracy but limited probabilistic calibration; Moirai-2 shows context-dependent and moderate performance, competitive in some settings but insufficiently reliable overall; and Lag-Llama consistently underperforms across disease targets and locations, making it an unreliable forecasting tool in its current form. Performance stratified by epidemic phase further shows that TSFMs share the same phase-dependent strengths and limitations observed in other forecasting approaches. The retrospective analysis of the 2024/25 season is consistent with results observed for 2025/26, supporting the robustness of our findings beyond a single epidemic season, while also highlighting that phase-specific performance can vary from season to season. Importantly, no single TSFM consistently outperforms all individual models and ensembles across all settings. This heterogeneity reflects what is routinely observed among the individual models submitted to forecasting hubs each week, where performance is similarly variable across contributing models; in this sense, TSFMs do not yet represent a paradigm shift but rather a new class of tools that can contribute to the field. This indicates that, at their current stage of maturity, these models cannot be a sole substitute for existing multi-model forecasting efforts. That said, at least some of them show competitive performance and can complement and facilitate current forecasting approaches. As with any forecasting tool, however, one should not treat TSFM outputs as inherently reliable: ongoing evaluation should be a standard part of any workflow that incorporates them. Continued season-to-season assessment will help track the impact and improvements of model updates as they are released, and how year-to-year variability in respiratory illness activity and severity affects performance. Efforts to incorporate the results of real-time evaluations like these into their training and development should be prioritized to improve the operational utility of these tools. This need for evaluation extends beyond recurrent respiratory disease forecasting, as TSFMs are general-purpose models that could also be applied to future health emergencies.

Beyond performance heterogeneity across models, we also observed structural issues in the outputs of some TSFMs, which required post-hoc correction before forecasts could be evaluated. Because several models do not natively produce all 23 required quantiles, interpolation was needed to derive the missing quantile levels. Most TSFMs produced negative values in some instances, which were set to zero. Additionally, a few TSFMs produced quantile forecasts that occasionally violated monotonicity, which we corrected by replacing flagged quantiles via linear interpolation between the nearest valid neighbors. These structural issues indicate that the raw outputs of some TSFMs are not yet directly suited for operational epidemic forecasting without additional post-processing. This is a practical concern: less technical users may not recognize or correct such issues, and could unknowingly deploy these outputs as-is, undermining downstream decisions.

Consistent with the official seasonal hub evaluations, 33 all scores were computed on the log scale following Bosse et al. 44 . Nonetheless, model rankings and relative scores reported here may differ from those in the published FluSight seasonal evaluation 33 for the following reasons. First, the pairwise comparison approach scores each model relative to all other models in the evaluation set. Adding the six TSFMs to the pool of hub models therefore changes the relative scores of every model, including the hub models. Second, our evaluation includes Puerto Rico, which is excluded from the official FluSight evaluation. Third, we define each forecast instance by reference date, location, and horizon; differences in how forecasts are grouped may affect the resulting relative scores. This work comes with limitations. First, we evaluated TSFMs exclusively in a zero-shot setting, providing past data as context and without any task-specific fine-tuning. Indeed, our goal was to characterize out-of-the-box performance. Nonetheless, future work should explore to what extent domain-specific fine-tuning can further improve performance. Relatedly, future work could also explore whether TSFMs can be trained or fine-tuned to improve phase-specific performance, for instance by prioritizing performance during key epidemic phases (e.g., pre-peak). The fact that some of the best-performing TSFMs in our evaluation showed comparatively strong performance during the growth phase suggests this could be a promising avenue for further development. Future work could also explore new forecasting targets beyond weekly hospital admissions, such as epidemic peak timing or growth rate. Also, the TSFMs evaluated here were provided only with NHSN hospital admissions data as context, without incorporating other surveillance indicators, such as emergency department visit data, that are included in some existing modeling approaches and could improve forecast accuracy. Future work should explore whether providing TSFMs with additional indicator data as covariates, where supported, can improve their forecasting performance. It is worth keeping in mind that we focused on six widely used and state-of-the-art TSFMs. However, this is a rapidly expanding field, and a broader set of models will be increasingly available. For this reason, future analyses should expand our performance evaluation to include newer versions and model architectures. 45 Finally, we acknowledge recent advances in a dedicated line of research aimed at developing domain-specific foundation models for epidemic forecasting. [46] [47] [48] While we deliberately focused on evaluating general-purpose TSFMs, a natural direction for future work is to evaluate these domain-specific foundation models and benchmark them against general-purpose TSFMs, individual hub contributors, and ensembles in an operational forecasting setting.

Overall, our results suggest that current TSFMs are not a single solution for operational shortterm epidemic forecasting. Collaborative modeling efforts and multi-model ensembles remain the strongest and most reliable strategy for communicating short-term forecasts and scenario projections to key stakeholders. This work provides early information for the epidemic modeling community on the potential and limitations of frontier TSFMs in operational forecasting settings and highlights the need for rigorous evaluation to make the most of their full potential and effectively integrate them into collective forecasting efforts.

4 Methods

Here, we describe the TSFMs selected for evaluation and key implementation details relevant to the epidemic forecasting task, followed by an overview of the collaborative forecasting hubs, the metrics used to evaluate their performance, and the methodologies used to further characterize and stratify these results. Although we do not formally submit forecasts to the hubs, we operate in the same real-time fashion, generating predictions weekly as new data become available. Each TSFM receives as input the historical time series of influenza and COVID-19 hospital admissions starting from the 2020/21 season. A pre-processing step was applied to models that required a complete, gap-free input sequence, filling any missing values via linear interpolation; a post-processing step was applied to models whose quantile outputs occasionally violated monotonicity, correcting them post hoc. An additional post-processing step was applied to models that did not natively produce all 23 required quantile levels; for those models, the missing quantiles were derived via interpolation. Finally, all models except TimesFM produced some negative quantile values, which were clipped to zero. The Supplementary Information (Sec. S4) provides full details on which models were affected by each pre-and post-processing step. All forecasts have been made publicly available at https://github.com/sfiandrino/epi-tsfm-evaluation.

4.1 Time series foundation models description

Chronos-2 is a time-series foundation model based on an encoder-only Transformer derived from the T5 architecture, 49 introduced by Amazon Web Services in 2025. 38 Chronos-2 is trained on a mixture of real-world and synthetic datasets. It incorporates temporal attention to capture long-range dependencies and seasonality and employs a group attention mechanism to share information across similar time series. Chronos-2 directly outputs quantile forecasts over multiple horizons, and this output format is well aligned with the probabilistic forecasting requirements of epidemic modeling. Since Chronos-2 quantile outputs occasionally violate monotonicity, we apply a post hoc correction in which flagged quantiles are replaced by linear interpolation between the nearest valid neighbors. We use the chronos-forecasting package (v2.2.1) with the pretrained model amazon/chronos-2.

Lag-Llama is an open-source TSFM for time series forecasting with official model releases in February 2024, based on a decoder-only autoregressive Transformer architecture designed for univariate probabilistic forecasting. 39 Its key design feature is the use of lagged values as input features, allowing each prediction to incorporate information from selected past observations beyond the most recent context. Predictions are generated via step-by-step autoregressive sampling, and the Transformer representations are passed to a Student's t-distribution head, from which quantile forecasts are obtained via sampling. The number of samples is a user-defined parameter; we set it to 100 to balance quantile estimate stability and computational feasibility in the operational forecasting context. We use the pretrained lag-llama model, downloaded from the Hugging Face Hub (time-series-foundation-models/Lag-Llama).

Moirai-2 is a TSFM introduced by Salesforce in 2025, based on a decoder-only autoregressive Transformer architecture. 40 Moirai-2 employs autoregressive multi-quantile decoding, propagating uncertainty across prediction steps rather than collapsing forecasts to a single value. It outputs quantile forecasts optimized via the quantile (pinball) loss, 40 providing a theoretically grounded approach to probabilistic forecasting that aligns with the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS). We note that Moirai-2 natively outputs 9 quantile levels (0.1, 0.2, …, 0.9), which is a subset of the 23 quantile levels required by the hub submission format. The remaining quantile levels were obtained by linear interpolation using the 9 available quantiles. Missing values in the input time series are imputed via linear interpolation before model input. 40 Since Moirai-2 quantile outputs occasionally violate monotonicity, we apply a post-hoc correction in which flagged quantiles are replaced via linear interpolation between the nearest valid neighbors. We use the Moirai2Forecast model from the uni2ts package (Salesforce AI Research).

TabPFN-TS is a tabular foundation model and differs from the sequence-based architecture of conventional TSFMs, introduced by Prior Labs in 2024, and officially released in 2025. 41, 50 It applies the regression variant of TabPFN-v2 51 to a tabular representation of the series built from explicit temporal features, including a running index, calendar-based variables, and automatically inferred seasonal components. Rather than learning temporal structure implicitly from raw sequences, the model relies on engineered features, offering a complementary forecasting approach to the other TSFMs evaluated in this study. TabPFN-TS supports probabilistic forecasting through direct quantile prediction, making it compatible with the submission format required by epidemic collaborative efforts. We note that TabPFN-TS natively outputs 9 quantile levels (0.1, 0.2, …, 0.9), which is a subset of the 23 quantile levels required by the hub submission format. The remaining quantile levels were obtained by linear interpolation using the 9 available quantiles. The input representation is constructed using three temporal feature transformers: a running index, calendar-based features, and automatically inferred seasonal features. Missing values are imputed via linear interpolation before model input, as the architecture requires a complete, gap-free sequence. 50 We use the tabpfn-time-series package (v1.0.7).

TimeGPT is a transformer-based TSFM developed by Nixtla in 2023, based on an encoderdecoder architecture with stacked layers, residual connections, and layer normalization. 42 TimeGPT is not fully open source; available descriptions indicate that the model was pretrained on 100 billion time-series observations spanning diverse temporal structures, including multiple seasonal patterns, irregular cycles, and varying noise and outlier intensity. 42 For uncertainty quantification, TimeGPT supports either direct quantile forecasting or prediction intervals via conformal prediction. Here, we extract all 23 quantile levels required by the hub submission format directly via the API's quantiles parameter, returning the corresponding percentiles of the predictive distribution, which align with the probabilistic forecasting requirements of epidemic modeling. Missing values are imputed via linear interpolation before model input, as the architecture requires a complete, gap-free sequence. 42 We use the nixtla package accessed via the TimeGPT API.

TimesFM is a decoder-only TSFM developed by Google Research for zero-shot forecasting and released in 2024. 43 It represents the input series as contiguous, non-overlapping patches and processes them through stacked causal self-attention layers. A key design feature is using an output patch length that exceeds the input patch length, thereby reducing the number of autoregressive iterations required for multi-step-ahead prediction. TimesFM also employs patch masking during training, exposing the model to variable context lengths, a useful property in epidemic forecasting where the amount of available historical data can vary across locations and targets. Probabilistic forecasts are generated through a dedicated output layer trained with quantile loss at each required probability level, directly producing quantile forecasts. TimesFM natively outputs 9 quantile levels (0.1, 0.2, …, 0.9), which is a subset of the 23 quantile levels required by the hub submission format. The remaining quantile levels were obtained by linear interpolation using the 9 available quantiles. We use the timesfm package installed from the official Google Research repository.

4.2 Collaborative hubs description

A collaborative hub is a consortium of independent research teams organized around a shared forecasting task, defined by a common target variable, time period, set of locations, and forecast horizons, in which each team contributes probabilistic predictions generated by its own model. 52 These forecasts are combined weekly into a multi-model ensemble, as combining outputs from multiple models leverages a long-standing tradition in forecasting and yields a more robust representation of consensus across different approaches than relying on any single model. 27 Within this framework, the hub plays a central role in coordinating activities, including the collection, archiving, evaluation, and synthesis of forecasts. 26 Modeling teams are required to submit weekly forecasts to the centralized hub, following a standardized format to ensure consistent aggregation and comparison across models. Typically, teams provide probabilistic forecasts in the form of quantiles.

In this study, we consider the U.S. collaborative hubs for short-term forecasts. FluSight 36 collects forecasts of weekly laboratory-confirmed influenza hospital admissions across 53 U.S. locations (50 states, Washington DC, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. national level), typically running from November through May. The COVID-19 Forecast Hub (CovidHub) 37 collects forecasts of weekly confirmed COVID-19 hospital admissions across the same 53 locations from November, operating on a rolling basis from November 2024 onwards. Confirmed weekly hospital admission data are officially released by the NHSN Weekly Hospital Respiratory Dataset. 35 The target dataset is updated with new data every Wednesday by midday (pending data availability). To ensure real-time forecasting, all forecasts must be submitted weekly by Wednesday end of day. For both hubs, modeling teams provide national-and jurisdiction-level probabilistic forecasts at 23 predefined quantile levels (0.010, 0.025, 0.050, …, 0.950, 0.975, 0.990), covering 0-to 3-weeks ahead of the reference week. This time window includes the four weeks after the most recent hospital admissions data. Teams are not required to submit predictions for all horizons or locations.

For both hubs, the ensemble model is generated by aggregating valid submissions from all models designated for inclusion in the ensemble, using the hubEnsembles package from the Hubverse framework, 53 and computing it as the quantile-level median across all eligible quantilebased submissions. The baseline model is neutral and serves as a performance benchmark against which both individual models and the ensemble can be evaluated. It provides a simple reference forecast where the median prediction at all future horizons equals the last observed value, and the predictive distribution is derived from the historical distribution of week-to-week changes in incidence.

4.3 Forecast evaluation

Scoring scale. Following Bosse et al. 44 , all scores are computed on the log-transformed scale. Before scoring, both forecast quantiles and observed values are transformed as log(y + 1), where the offset avoids undefined values at zero. Scoring on the log scale approximates a measure of relative rather than absolute error. This stabilizes score variance across locations and prevents high-burden jurisdictions from dominating aggregate comparisons. Accordingly, WIS and AE (Eqs. 1-3) and the relative WIS and relative AE derived from them (Eqs. 5-7) are computed on log-transformed quantities, and expressed in the text as log WIS, log AE, relative log WIS and relative log AE.

Weighted Interval Score (WIS).

The WIS is a proper scoring rule that evaluates both the accuracy and calibration of probabilistic forecasts. It summarizes how well a forecast distribution captures observed outcomes by combining two properties: sharpness, i.e., the narrowness of the prediction intervals, and calibration, i.e., the agreement between predicted and realized probabilities. Well-calibrated and sharp forecasts achieve lower WIS values. The WIS is a standard tool for comparing probabilistic forecasts in the context of infectious disease ensemble forecasting. 34 Formally, for a given forecast distribution F with predictive median m, and K central (1-)×100% prediction intervals defined by lower and upper bounds and , the interval score (IS) at level is defined as: , where y denotes the observed value and 1{•} is an indicator function.

The overall WIS is then obtained as a weighted average of the absolute error of the predictive median and the interval scores across all considered levels: ,

Following standard practice, 34 we used K = 11 central prediction intervals corresponding to = 0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, and 0.90.

Absolute Error (AE).

Relative performance. We compute the relative performance for WIS and AE using a pairwise comparison approach in which the relative skill of a model m with respect to the set of all other models {1, …, M}, including the baseline model, is considered. 26 For each pair of models m and m′, we compute the pairwise relative WIS and relative AE skill as: where and (resp. and ) are the average of WIS or AE of the model (resp. ) computed using all available forecasts where both model and model participated.

Then, for each model , we compute the geometric mean across the different models:

Finally, to compare model performance with respect to the baseline model, we divide +by the result obtained for the baseline, named + -:

The obtained value + represents the relative WIS or relative AE of model rescaled to the baseline model, such that the baseline has a value of 1. It follows that + < 1 indicates that the model performs better than the baseline, and + > 1 indicates that the model performs worse than the baseline. All scores are computed on the log-transformed scale 44 as described above.

Tertile classification.

To contextualize model performance beyond raw relative scores, we additionally classified models into tertiles based on their rank across all M models evaluated within each challenge (for both relative log WIS and relative log AE). Models were ranked from best to worst-performing (i.e., from lowest to highest), and divided into three groups of approximately equal size using the 33.3rd and 66.7th percentiles of the rank distribution as cutoffs. The top tertile includes the best-ranked third of models, the middle tertile the next third, and the bottom tertile the remaining, worst-ranked third. When M is not evenly divisible by three, the remaining model(s) were sequentially assigned to the higher tertiles (top, then middle), so that the bottom tertile was never larger than the other two.

4.4 Disease trend classification

To characterize model performance across different epidemic phases, we developed a method to classify trends in influenza and COVID-19 activity based on historical data. We adapted the methodology originally developed by the CDC for influenza activity, 54 applying the same approach to both diseases using hospital admission data from NHSN. 35 We derived weekly rates per 100,000 population and computed the week-to-week difference in these rates for each season, considering all available historical data from the 2022/23 season onward, to exclude COVID-19 seasons in which activity patterns may have been distorted by pandemic period dynamics (2019/20, 2020/21, 2021/22). From the resulting distribution of rate differences, we established five categories of change: large decrease, decrease, stable, increase, and large increase. We derived a single set of thresholds using national-level (U.S.) rate differences as the reference distribution, based on the 5th, 25th, 75th, and 95th percentiles, which we used as cutoffs to define the trend categories. Specifically, differences greater than the 25th percentile and lower than the 75th percentile were classified as stable; differences between the 75th (inclusive) and 95th percentiles were classified as an increase; differences between the 5th and 25th (inclusive) percentiles were classified as a decrease; and differences at or below the 5th percentile or at or above the 95th percentile were classified as a large decrease or large increase, respectively. For each jurisdiction, weeks with an absolute change of <10 hospital admissions were classified as stable, to limit the impact of reporting delays and random fluctuations.

Based on these criteria, for FluSight, stable weeks were defined as a change in weekly rate ≥ -0.09 to < 0.04 influenza-associated hospitalizations/100,000, or as weeks with an absolute difference of <10 hospital admissions. Increases were defined as a positive change in weekly rate ≥ 0.04 to < 1.59/100,000, and large increases as a positive change ≥ 1.59/100,000. Decreases were defined as a negative change in weekly rate > -1.39 to < -0.09/100,000, and large decreases as a negative change ≤ -1.39/100,000. For CovidHub, stable weeks were defined as a change in weekly rate ≥ -0.30 to < 0.12 COVID-19-associated hospitalizations/100,000, or as weeks with an absolute difference of <10 hospital admissions. Increases were defined as a positive change in weekly rate ≥ 0.12 to < 0.86/100,000, and large increases as a positive change ≥ 0.86/100,000. Decreases were defined as a negative change in weekly rate > -0.77 to < -0.30/100,000, and large decreases as a negative change ≤ -0.77/100,000.

In the Supplementary Information (Sec. S5), we present a more detailed visualization of the resulting trend classification applied to the U.S. national curve for both diseases. We also conducted a sensitivity analysis to evaluate our threshold-derivation approach. For influenza, we compared the obtained thresholds and trend classifications against those officially reported by the CDC in ref. 54, which were instead derived from an independent surveillance system (FluSurv-NET). Despite this difference in derivation, agreement between our influenza trend classifications and those obtained using the original CDC thresholds for the 2024/25 and 2025/26 seasons was high, with a percentage of agreement of 89%. We also quantified the agreement using Cohen's Kappa, a statistic that measures inter-rater agreement while accounting for the level of agreement expected by chance alone. Kappa values above 0.80 are conventionally considered near-perfect agreement. The resulting Kappa of 0.83 supports the validity of our adapted approach for classifying disease trends.

4.5 Use of AI tools

We used Claude (Anthropic) to assist with manuscript preparation in the following ways. We used it as a coding assistant for the scripts used to plot the figures. The authors reviewed the plotting scripts and ran them on the study data. No figure or image was generated by AI. Claude was also used for copy editing of author-written text, limited to wording and grammar. No AI tool generated scientific content or produced the analyses, results, or conclusions. We used the time series foundation models subject to the research to produce weekly forecasts on publicly available data. The authors take full responsibility for this article's content.
